title: Radiant Floor Heating In Theory and Practice

findings.antecedent: Floor surface temperature change of 5 K (9°F)
findings.quote: a 5 K (9°F) change of the floor surface tem- perature will have the same effect as chang- ing the air temperature by 2 K (3.6°F).

findings.antecedent: One degree change of floor temperature
findings.consequent: Effect on mean radiant temperature (and operative temperature) compared to a change of ceiling temperature
findings.quote: one degree change of the floor temperature will have 2.5 times the effect on the mean radiant temperature (and operative tem- perature) than a change of the ceiling temperature.5

findings.antecedent: Floor heating system
findings.consequent: Air temperature required to reach the same level of operative temperature compared to a 100% convective heating system
findings.quote: Compared to a 100% convective heat- ing system (warm air heating), a floor heating system can reach the same level of operative temperature at a lower air temperature (Figure 15).

findings.antecedent: Floor heating system (resulting in lower air temperature for same operative temperature)
findings.quote: Therefore, there will not be any significant reduction of trans- mission heat loss. It will, however, result in a lower ventilation heat loss.

findings.antecedent: High ventilation rates (e.g., industrial storage areas, hangars) combined with radiant heating
findings.quote: In buildings with high ventilation rates, such as industrial storage areas, hangars, etc., this has a significant influence on energy consumption and supports the use of radi- ant heating.

findings.antecedent: Modern well-insulated and tight residential buildings
findings.consequent: Reduction in ventilation heat loss due to lower air temperature with radiant heating
findings.quote: In modern well-insulated and tight residential buildings, this effect is minor because the difference between mean radiant and air temperature is relatively small.

findings.antecedent: Increased insulation of buildings (walls/windows) and decreased heat loads
findings.consequent: Difference in thermal environment between various heating systems
findings.quote: By increasing insulation of buildings (walls/win- dows), and thus, decreasing heat loads, the difference between systems is less.

findings.antecedent: Floor temperature in occupied zone (rooms with sedentary and/or standing occupants wearing normal shoes)
findings.quote: a floor temperature range of 19°C to 29°C (66°F to 84°F) is recommended in the occupied zone for rooms with sedentary and/or standing occupants wear- ing normal shoes.

findings.antecedent: Floor temperature for heating
findings.quote: For heating, the maximum temperature is 29°C (84°F), and for cooling, the minimum temperature is 19°C (66°F).

findings.antecedent: Design floor temperature outside the occupied zone (within 1 m [3 ft] from outside walls/windows)
findings.quote: In the European standard, it is acceptable to use 35°C (95°F) as the design floor temperature outside the occupied zone, i.e., within 1 m (3 ft) from outside walls/windows.

findings.antecedent: Occupants with bare feet (e.g., bathrooms, swimming pools, dressing rooms) and floor material
findings.quote: In spaces where occupants may have bare feet (bathrooms, swim- ming pools, dressing rooms), the optimal floor temperature for comfort also depends on the floor material.10

findings.antecedent: Radiant floor heating
findings.consequent: Vertical air temperature differences from floor to ceiling
findings.quote: One of the main features of radiant floor heating is the uni- form temperature conditions from floor to ceiling.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating and large wall panel heater under a window compared to more convective systems
findings.quote: Floor heating and the large wall panel heater under the window have a uniform temperature profile. The more convective systems have larger differences.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating (for a given operative temperature of 22°C [72°F]) compared to other heating systems
findings.quote: Figure 1 shows that the 22°C (72°F) operative temperature, using floor heating, was obtained at 1 K to 1.5 K (1.8°F to 2.7°F) lower air temperature than the other systems.

findings.antecedent: Increased stratification in high ceiling spaces (e.g., industrial workplaces, atriums, hangars)
findings.quote: In high ceil- ing spaces, such as industrial workplaces, atriums, and hangars, increased stratification significantly increases heat loss because of the increase in average space temperature.

findings.antecedent: Modern buildings with cold windows
findings.quote: there are seldom problems with radiant asym- metry from cold windows in modern buildings.

findings.antecedent: Air velocity lower than 0.18 m/s (36 fpm) at design conditions
findings.consequent: Need to compensate with heating below the window (to prevent downdraft)
findings.quote: If the air velocity is lower than the 0.18 m/s (36 fpm) at design conditions, it is unnecessary to compensate with heating below the window.

findings.antecedent: Need to compensate for downdraft + floor heating design
findings.quote: If needed, floor heating can be de- signed with a higher surface temperature at the wall/window (smaller pipe distance, higher water temperature).

findings.antecedent: Radiant floor heating (leading to lower air temperature)
findings.quote: the air temperature can be kept lower than in “standard” houses. This has the advantage that the relative humidity in winter may be a little higher.

findings.antecedent: Lower air temperatures
findings.quote: Also, studies show12 that people perceive air quality to be better at lower air temperatures.

findings.antecedent: Higher surface temperatures (from floor heating)
findings.consequent: Chance for condensation and mold growth
findings.quote: Due to the higher surface temperatures, there is less chance for condensation and mold growth. Floor heating also prevents cold corners.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating compared to other heating systems
findings.consequent: Favorable living conditions for house dust mites
findings.quote: The German Allergy and Asthma Association13 has produced a study that shows that floor heating reduces the favorable living conditions for house dust mites compared to other heat- ing systems.

findings.antecedent: Higher temperatures in carpets and mattresses
findings.quote: Higher temperatures in carpets and mattresses decrease the relative humidity.

findings.antecedent: Mites seeking upper areas
findings.consequent: Ease of removal by vacuum cleaners
findings.quote: Also, because mites seek the upper areas, they are more easily removed by vacuum cleaners.

findings.antecedent: Korean houses (with floor heating) compared to Japanese houses
findings.quote: Another study found a lower level of dust mites in Korean houses than in Japanese houses.14 This was attributed to the same effect, but was not directly verified.

findings.antecedent: Radiant heating systems compared to convective heating systems
findings.quote: Radiant heating systems result in less transportation of dust compared to convective heating systems.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating
findings.consequent: Need for cleaning heat emitters/carpets, source for emitting pollutants, sink source for pollutants, helpful for allergies
findings.quote: Also, floor heating does not require cleaning heat emitters. Carpets are not as necessary when using floor heating, which eliminates a source for emitting pollutants and a sink source. This is especially helpful for people with allergies.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating with 29°C (84°F) floor temperature and 20°C (68°F) room temperature in the occupied zone
findings.quote: The maximum capacity in the occupied zone is about 100 W/m² (29°C [84°F]) floor temperature, 20°C (68°F) room temperature.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating with 35°C (96°F) floor temperature within 1 m (3 ft) from outside walls/windows and 20°C (68°F) room temperature
findings.quote: A 20°C (68°F) room temperature results in a heat output of 165 W/m².

findings.antecedent: Type of floor covering (tiles, wood, carpet)
findings.quote: This maximum heating capacity is indepen- dent of the type of floor covering (tiles, wood, carpet).

findings.antecedent: Thermal resistance of floor covering, system type, and pipe spacing
findings.consequent: Required water temperature to obtain maximum heating capacity
findings.quote: The re- quired water temperature to obtain the maximum heating capacity is, however, dependent on the thermal resistance of the floor cov- ering and other factors such as system type and pipe spacing.

findings.antecedent: Floor cooling with 26°C (78.8°F) room temperature and 20°C (68°F) floor temperature
findings.consequent: Maximum cooling capacity in most buildings
findings.quote: In most buildings a maximum cooling capacity at 26°C (78.8°F) room temperature and 20°C (68°F) floor tem- perature is then 42 W/m².

findings.antecedent: Direct sunlight on the floor (e.g., in atriums, airports, entrance halls) with floor cooling
findings.quote: Direct sunlight on the floor (as in atriums, airports, entrance halls) can cause the cooling capac- ity to be higher than 100 W/m2.16,17

findings.antecedent: Well-insulated buildings combined with changes in internal loads (occupants, lighting, equipment, direct sunlight)
findings.quote: The low heat loss in well-insulated build- ings means that changes in internal loads have a higher impact on the room temperature than in buildings with standard insula- tion.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating systems (often having higher mass compared to other heating systems)
findings.consequent: Risk for overheating and additional heat loss
findings.quote: As floor heating systems often have a higher mass compared to other heating systems, it is often claimed that using floor heating means a greater risk for overheating and additional heat loss. However, several studies have found the opposite to be true.

findings.antecedent: Standard floor heating systems with tubes embedded in concrete compared to low temperature radiator systems (with controls)
findings.quote: The results showed that, for both heating systems, the controls easily kept the room temperature within acceptable limits. There was no difference between the two systems.

findings.antecedent: Self-control effect of heating systems
findings.quote: This self-control is only valid for hydronic floor heat- ing systems and not electrically heated floor systems.

findings.antecedent: Individual room control compared to central control only (for heating systems)
findings.quote: The studies showed a 15% to 30% energy savings by using an individual room control compared to a central control only.

findings.antecedent: Night setback used with floor heating and boost heating in the reheat period
findings.quote: If night setback is used with floor heating, it is recommended to use boost heating in the reheat period in the morning to in- crease the floor heating. Reheat heating using a floor heating system must start earlier in the morning (than a radiator system), however the system can then be turned off earlier in the evening.

findings.antecedent: Individual room temperature controls
findings.quote: Due to the improved comfort when using individual room control and the possible energy savings, the installation of individual room temperature controls is recommended.

findings.antecedent: Ability for occupants to individually adjust the temperature in a room
findings.quote: Besides the energy benefits, it is essential for thermal com- fort for occupants to be able to individually adjust the tem- perature in a room.

findings.antecedent: Low-temperature heating
findings.consequent: Distribution losses and efficiency of heat generation
findings.quote: Using low-tem- perature heating is beneficial regarding distribution losses and efficiency of heat generation.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating
findings.consequent: Efficiency of boilers (especially modern condensing boilers)
findings.quote: The highest efficiency of boil- ers, especially modern condensing boilers, is obtained by floor heating.

findings.antecedent: Low-temperature heating system (e.g., floor heating)
findings.consequent: Efficiency of heat pumps as a solar collector
findings.quote: Also, the efficiency of heat pumps as a solar collector is much better with a low-temperature heating system such as floor heating.

findings.antecedent: Floor system (as a high-temperature heating system)
findings.consequent: Efficiency for a reversible heat pump or chiller
findings.quote: Because a floor system is a high-temperature heating system, it enables a higher efficiency for a reversible heat pump or chiller.

findings.antecedent: Floor cooling system combined with an air system
findings.quote: The floor system takes care of most of the sensible load while the air system takes care of the latent load.

findings.antecedent: Lowered dew point in the space and high return water temperature (18-20°C [64.4-68°F]) of the floor system (with floor cooling)
findings.consequent: Cooling capacity and efficiency of a refrigeration machine
findings.quote: At the same time, the dew point in the space will be lowered resulting in a higher cooling capacity for the floor system. Also, the high return water temperature (18°C to 20°C [64.4°F to 68°F]) of the floor system increases the efficiency of a refrigeration machine.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating vs. radiators (installation cost)
findings.quote: Overall, the difference was within ±10%, but several installers charged a higher overhead for floor heating, because they could sell it as a more comfortable and energy efficient heating system.

findings.antecedent: Hydronic radiant floor heating
findings.consequent: Efficient use of space, cleaning requirement, noise generation, drafts, duct usage, temperature distribution, system temperature
findings.quote: The advantages of hydronic radiant floor heating include the efficient use of space and that cleaning is not required. Also, the system does not produce noise, cause drafts or use ducts. The system has uniform temperature distribution and is a low-temperature heating system.

findings.antecedent: Radiant floor heating system
findings.consequent: Indoor air temperature required for same operative temperature and ventilation heat loss compared to more convective heating systems
findings.quote: In a radiant floor heating system, the required operative temperature may be obtained at a lower indoor air temperature. This reduces ventilation heat loss compared to more convec- tive heating systems.

findings.antecedent: Convective vs. radiant heating systems
findings.quote: The transmission heat loss is more re- lated to operative temperature and is more or less the same for convective and radiant systems.

findings.antecedent: Combination of floor heating self-control and a room thermostat in well-insulated buildings
findings.consequent: Efficiency of control for variations in internal loads (occupants, lighting, direct sunlight)
findings.quote: The combination of the self-control of floor heating systems combined with a room thermostat makes an efficient control for variations in internal loads even in well-insulated buildings.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating (due to low water temperatures used)
findings.quote: Floor heating increases the efficiency of heat generators due to the low water temperatures used.

findings.antecedent: Hydronic floor cooling system
findings.quote: A hydronic floor cooling system provides sensible cooling without generating noise or drafts.

findings.antecedent: Direct sunlight on the floor (with floor cooling)
findings.quote: In spaces with direct sunlight on the floor, the cool- ing capacity is significantly higher.
